The Benesh Movement Notation 
notated score can be used for study, research, and mounting. No one 
would give a musician a disc or tape and say 'perform this." Not only 
would it be impossible, but interpretative artists must work direct 
from the composer's score and usually prefer not to see or hear other 
interpretations for fear of influencing their own. 
The film or tape is the record of a particular performance of a 
particular production in which particular artists gave their particular 
interpretations on that particular occasion. It is a very valuable his- 
torical document, giving the style, interpretation, et cetera, and li- 
braries of dance should contain both the score and the films or video 
tapes in the same way that music libraries contain both the score 
and tapes. (There could be many different tapes for each score.) 
The position is paralleled in scientific work in which the film is 
only a means of storing visual phenomena. Analytical and compara- 
tive research, and especially creative research, demands an appropri- 
ate notation for mental manipulation. Notation is the tool of the brain 
and its efficacy in any research or study determines the progress of 
that subject. Science, engineering, and technology have only been 
made possible by their notation, mathematics, and the same is equally 
true in the case of music. Similarly, a computer can only work through 
a notation. Work on any subject without the use of a proper notation 
cannot claim serious respect and is certainly not academic. 
Hospitals using choreography emphatically endorse Professor Mi- 
lani's findings (1968) that a film is not suitable for the purpose, be- 
cause of its ambiguity and limited validity, and that in fact, it is 
just a means of storing visual phenomena. 
An official survey of professional dance companies also found the 
shortcomings of film or video tape too great for use. These shortcom- 
ings are: masking, by person's own body and limbs, one person cov- 
ering another, shadows, props, costumes, et cetera; ambiguities caused 
by lighting, camera angle, lens used; errors and changes, especially if 
recorded after a lapse of time; it cannot show stage plans, groups, et 
cetera; when improvisation is included, it cannot distinguish what is 
set and what is improvised. Neither can it record improvisation limita- 
tion instructions. 
As will be seen, the question opens up many important issues which 
cannot be adequately dealt with here.

your system?

Movement Notation and Choreology : 
1947- 
1955--evolving and completing of movement notation. 
1955-adoption 
by the Royal Ballet and commence teaching in the Royal 
Ballet School and other leading schools.

by Rudolf and Joan Benesh.

Will you give a brief, non-technical review of the system? 
First, as we record what we see, we must decide a viewpoint. This 
can either be from in ftont of the subject or behind him. From the 
very start, recording from behind the subject's back has been estab- 
lished, as this enables the writer and reader to identify themselves 
with the subject, which in itself has advantages in medical and scien- 
tific records and studies. 
Supposing you were to ask a person to press himself face inwards 
against a wall and take up any position in which every part of him, 
so far as possible, is in contact with the wall. By marking the exact 
spots where his four extremities contacted the wall and by marking 
the position of a bent knee or elbow, he will be able to go away and 
return to the posture at will. The tilt and turn of the head and body 
could also be added by single lines and if the subject were to hold a 
piece of chalk in one hand and move his arm about, we would have 
a record of the path of movement on the wall. If now we calibrate 
the wall by drawing horizontal lines so that the top one is level with 
the top of the head, the next is at shoulder height, the next at the 
waist and another at the knee, the floor being the bottom line, we 
have a five-line stave and no longer need the subject to return to 
show us the position but can accurately read it when written at any 
size. 
This is of course two-dimensional, but it is a simple matter to in- 
corporate the three dimensions of space (see answer to the next ques- 
tion). As we plot points in space, so these must also be plotted as 
points in time. Thus the concept of rhythm in dance and movement 
generally is very different from that of music. Firstly, the scale is 
different. Furthermore, whereas in music one has a note or chord 
with duration in time followed by another, in movement this has no

## Page 6

The Benesh Movement Notation 
meaning whatsoever. In movement notation we have a time signature 
giving the metronomic pulse beat and the division into metric cycles, 
such as bars in music. Within this matrix the salient points in space 
are fixed as points in time whether these be on the pulse beat or on 
a sub-beat. 
All this is basically simple, but it is because of the basic simplicity 
of the notation that the full complexity of movement can be dealt 
with simply. It is not possible to give a complete view of the system 
without diagrams and I suggest you refer to either articles or one of 
the above-mentioned books. 
What are the notation system's fundamental assumptions and ap- 
proaches? 
The approaches are linguistic, cybernetic, and ergonomic. Axiom 
number one is a linguistic notation principle based on the fact that 
different forms of communication or language are perceived through 
one or other of our senses and the need for the appropriate notation 
in all cases to be geared to the working of that particular sense organ. 
It must also have a logical structure derived from the particular 
medium. For example, speech is perceived through the ear and the 
logical structure is phonetic. Consequently, the only effective speech 
notation must be phonetically based. Music is also perceived through 
the ears and is therefore an oral art and its logical structure is based 
on pitch, interval, and duration. Movement, on the other hand, is 
perceived through the eyes and dance must accordingly be one of the 
visual arts since contact with the audience can only be through their 
eyes. Therefore, a movement notation must be visual and based on 
the logical structure of visual perception. 
The second axiom arises from the first. It is the principle of linear 
perspective and utilizes the manner in which the eye projects three- 
dimensional objects onto its two-dimensional retina. This has long 
since been reduced to mathematics, and the notation simplifies the 
rather complex subject by the application of parallel projection onto 
a "picture plane" which is the stave of notation. This 3-D representa- 
tion gives rise to the need for three basic signs. Signs, not symbols, 
which plot points in three-dimensional space on the matrix or five- 
line stave. This utilizes simple Cartesian geometry with its x, y, and z 
coordinates for plotting positions. Since the limbs are of fixed length, 
the z coordinate is not required. That is to say that the distance in 
front or behind the body is conditioned. By adding to this three-di- 
mensional representation of space, the dimension of time, it is pos- 
sible to trace the actual path of movement of an object. These four- 
dimensional representations are called movement lines, which by 
manipulation can reduce enormous complexity of movement to sim- 
vlicitv. 
 hi premises are the three basic signs and the matrix or five-line 
stave. By application of the concept that a cross equals a bend or tilt, 
and arising from this, that a tilt to the left means left, and vice-versa, 
and the use of strict logic, consistency, and ergonomics, the manipu-

## Page 7

lation of signs gives rise to a vast vocabulary. One further concept 
introduces contact with objects and this gives rise to a vocabulary of 
literally many thousands of possibilities with no addition of new 
signs. 
However complex the situation, the resulting sign remains simple 
and necessarily tiny since it still plots a position in space or on the 
body. The use of the five-line stave as used in music has many ad- 
vantages. Writing and reading from left to right has its obvious ergo- 
nomic advantage and is also the generally accepted convention for the 
flow of time. This is of paramount 2mportance where correlation with 
other notation, such as music, is required. Why five lines? There is no 
musical reason why music chose five, in fact it has used less, but 
never more. The reason would appear to be that five lines is the 
maximum number that the eye can read accurately with speed. Fur- 
thermore, five lines give the half and quarters which is ideal for visual 
purposes and for representing the human figure. So far this deals 
only with the notation or alphabet. The linguistic structure of move- 
ment language is another fascinating subject with the correct "spell- 
ing" to be determined for postures (words), steps (compound words), 
syntax (the order of signs, words, et cetera), grammar, with its prin- 
ciples of redundancy and conditioning, and the resulting vocabulary 
which must be ergonomic-that 
is, easily written with a line in a 
cursive manner from left to right. 
How accurate is the system? 
The notation is elastic and therefore is as accurate as is required. 
The normal l/t inch stave, giving a frame of 1/4 square inch, is as 
accurate as a trained recorder can cope with, and leaves a marginal 
reserve for all general purposes. For medical and neurological research 
and cerebral palsy patients' records, where details of body displace- 
ment as well as very precise differences of movement are important, 
a I-inch stave is used. This increases the matrix area by four times 
and its volume by eight times without increasing the size of the signs 
used. This accordingly increases the accuracy by eight times. In 
work-study, where detail of finger, hand, and arm movement is im- 
portant, the use of a so-called waist or hip stave is used, according 
to whether the operator is sitting at a desk or standing at a bench. 
This makes use of the normal stave but effectively increases the vol- 
ume by eight times and similarly the accuracy. These techniques more 
than cover the accuracy required, and no further modification has 
been called for, but it can be seen that by combining both the above 
techniques an increase in volume and therefore of definition or ac- 
curacy could be by eight times eight or sixty-four times. 
What do you see t o  be the basic strengths of the system in comparison 
to others in use? 
In order to be professionalIy viable, a notation must be practical. 
That is to say, economic in time-that 
is, rapid in use, economic in

## Page 8

The Benesh Movement Notation 
space, universal and comprehensive, accurate and reliable, and above 
all, simple. The only solution, as explained earlier, is a visual notation 
based on linguistic and ergonomic principles. This also makes it 
objective, with no philosophical or other bias. It also enables notation 
to break through what I call the linguistic barrier between alphabet 
and language; the key being simplicity through complexity. In the 
present case this has made Choreology possible, and the development 
of movement languages. Hence its success in the professional world 
of dance, medicine, et cetera. An official investigation by the National 
Foundation for the Arts and Humanities, USA, states: "Only the 
Benesh method, however, has been put to viable, wide-scale use in 
the professional dance theater." 
Does the system take into account movement qualities as well as 
movement quantities? 
Yes, it does as proved in its use in the theater, medical, work-study, 
scientific research, and education. This question is important as there 
appears to be some misunderstanding on the subject. Qualities of 
movement are closely tied up with dynamics on the one hand, and 
interpretation on the other. By interpretation, I mean that of the 
performing artist when ihterpreting the score. 
When dealing with the arts, this poses the difficult question of 
where to draw the line between detailed instruction of execution and 
how much freedom the artist is allowed for interpretation. Where the 
composer prepares the score he decides for himself, but where the 
score is prepared by another, perhaps without recourse to the com- 
poser, as is often the case in choreography, then it must be decided 
what is basic choreography and what is interpretation and produc- 
tion. The latter are often added to the score as such. Where this 
demarcation is made not only differs with different choreographers 
and composers, but also with fashion. The history of this in music 
is most illuminating. 
The correct use of dynamics also requires knowledge and experi- 
ence. Much of the dynamic quality is so intrinsic in the precise re- 
cording of the actual movement, its exact path, pace, and change 
of pace, that with a precise notation there is often very little to add. 
It has been found that during the course of developing a new move- 
ment language, it starts off with large doses of dynamic and quality 
indications which with progress gradually fall away until, when 
fully developed, there are surprisingly few. Even in such studies as 
the movement of spastic children, where one would expect a great 
deal, co-workers are always surprised by the lack of such markings. 
The reason also lies in the proper understanding of dynamics. The 
body is a very efficient machine, especially when used in dance and 
athletics. That is to say, it expends the minimum amount of energy 
for the maximum of movement. In a well-executed movement, only 
that amount of energy is used to move the limb, body, or object, and 
no more or less. If more is used in order to convey relaxation or flop -

## Page 9

Quest 
piness, or the extent of spasticity or flaccidity, then the degree of 
these must be indicated. Floppiness in a movement, that is the re- 
laxing of muscle tone, will result in a decrease of efficiency and a 
probable increase in energy used, like lifting a floppy rather than a 
rigid body. 
Language conventions also provide redundancy and conditioning 
factors which can be eliminated. Each convention also has its inter- 
pretation motivations: for example, those of the various schools of 
modern dance. And these should be understood and indicated as is 
done in music. 
However, it must be remembered that dance is a visual art and 
what the audience does not see will not get over to them. So all in- 
dications of quality of movement are to enable the dancer to more 
correctly execute the particular movement. The notator must record 
it as seen, not as felt. 
Is your system universally applicable to all forms of movement? 
As a pure, objective movement notation, the system is universally 
applicable to all forms of movement. 
Is it more suitable than the others for certain forms of movement? 
It has been proved more suitable than others for all forms of move- 
ment. 
In what ways may the system be used? 
The system may be used for recording details of facial expression, 
eye and finger movements, complex groups of people, stage patterns, 
teams, and work groups. It can record babies from birth, children, 
athletes, dancers, spastics, other primates, the multiple arms of 
Indian deities, and it can be adapted for animals. It is essential in any 
study in which any such movement is concerned. Most important, it 
is a research tool, various techniques having been developed, and 
also a creative tool of composition. The latter has been developed to 
a high and fascinating degree, only possible through a visual nota- 
tion. 
What questions about your notation system do you find most difficult 
to answer? 
I find it difficult to explain the linguistic basis of the notation and 
the growth of movement language out of it, as this is a very new 
branch of linguistic discipline. 
Another question I find difficult to answer is why education gen- 
erally does not, like the other professional worlds, understand the 
value and importance of notation, when only notation can give a 
subject what is called academic repectability. 
Is there anything in terms of movement you find especially difficult to 
deal with when using the system? 
No. The technical staff of the institute have regular technical meet-

ings and there are also regular meetings of choreologists, many com-

There are interesting problems of correlation with unnotated data, 
for example, in electronic music which has not been notated. How- 
ever, this is being done every day in dance companies. 
Where is the system taught? Please cite a few  laces where it is in use. 
There are 285 qualified teachers and there are 81 professionally 
qualified choreologists, some 50 of whom are on the staff of profes- 
sional dance companies, hospitals, universities and the like through- 
out the world. In fact, the demand for professional choreologists con- 
tinues to exceed the supply. Several hospitals are requiring choreolo- 
gists to join various research teams. Among the professional dance 
companies and universities with choreologists on their staffs are the 
following: The Royal Ballet has six and there are two at the School, 
Ballet Rambert, and School, Northern Dance Theater. London's Festi- 
val Ballet, Scottish Theater Ballet, New York City Ballet, United 
States International University, San Diego has two, the Canadian Na- 
tional Ballet and School has three, York University, Toronto also has 
one, Cape Town University, Pact Ballet, Johannesburg, The Austra- 
lian Ballet Company and School, The Academy of Ballet, Brisbane, 
The New Zealand Ballet Company, The Royal Swedish Ballet, The 
Norwegian National Ballet Company, The Deutsche Oper Ballet, The 
National Theatre, Munich, the Staatstheatre, Stuttgart, Zurich Oper 
Ballet, Net National Theater, Amsterdam, Belgium Institute of Ballet, 
The Brabant Conservatorium, Holland, The Develet Opera va Ba- 
lesi, Ankara, Guys Hospital, London. In addition, the Institute of 
ChoreoIogy has ten choreologists on its staff, each specializing in a 
particular application. 
How much training does one need to become competent in the use of 
the system? 
This question cannot be directly answered because one is not 
taught notation as such but the language to which it has been applied. 
One does not teach a child the alphabet, one teaches him to read and 
write a particular language using the alphabet. The actual alphabet or 
notation is very simple, the number of signs being basically three 
from which all the others are derived. But this alone is of little use. A 
notator must be an expert in the language he is recording. The two 
basic subjects of Choreology are ballet and modern dance (based on 
American modern dance); other subjects include jazz, character, folk, 
ethnic, historical, Indian dance, music, art (specifically eye training

## Page 11

comparable to a musician's ear training), anatomy, physiology, ki- 
neseology, composition, and other subjects according to application 
if non-dance. The Institute has a three year full-time course for the 
training of professional choreologists, who are experts in a wide 
variety of movement studies. There are other briefer and specific 
courses and an introductory correspondence course. 
Do you feel there is a need for agreement to adopt a single notation 
system or are there advantages in continuing to use several different 
systems? 
The answer to this question is that one universal system will in- 
evitably be accepted and used as already exists in the professional 
dance world. 
What is the future of notation in general and your system in particu- 
lar ? 
Since the development of any subject, whether in science, art, or 
technology, is dependent upon the efficacy of its notation, dance is 
already in every way being put on the same basis as music through 
the use of notation. All other subjects concerned with movement will 
likewise become exact and developed subjects. 
Music as we know it today was only made possible by notation; the 
technique of counterpoint, harmony, and orchestration could only be 
worked out on paper as could the fugue and sonata forms, which 
made possible the larger symphonic developments. 
When choreographers are trained, as are musicians, with notation 
as a creative tool, I anticipate great developments in the technique of 
composition, which are to some extent built into the notation. This is 
equally true of all subjects concerned with movement studies. Each 
will only find its full potential through the creative use of notation. 
This opens whole worlds of possibilities in which so much, if not 
everything, is yet to be done.
